assessment.nobel_worthiness: Political economics gave the field a unified, theory-plus-evidence framework for how electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity and fiscal institutions shape policy and development. It changed how economists treat institutions as endogenous and analyzable, and it has had broad influence across public economics, development and comparative politics.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini built the constitutional and electoral-rule program and wrote the synthesizing book. Besley's work on state capacity, accountability and the institutional foundations of development is closely linked to it. Together they plausibly form a coherent trio. Other contributors (e.g., Acemoglu, Robinson and Alesina) are either outside this credited set or have already been recognized, which complicates the framing.
assessment.maturity: Core work dates from the 1990s and 2000s and has been tested and extended for twenty years or more, so the contribution is well matured. The award would be timely rather than premature.
uncertainties: Overlap with the institutions prize of 2024 may reduce appetite for a second institutions-themed award.
Some of the empirical cross-country evidence on constitutions is contested.
Attribution boundaries with other political-economy scholars are not fully clear from the longlist alone.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki and Moore's 'Credit Cycles' formalized how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. It is a foundational mechanism in modern macro-finance and was highly influential after the 2008 crisis, in both academic work and policy discussion.
assessment.attribution: The core model is clearly credited to Kiyotaki and Moore. Gertler and Gilchrist's financial-accelerator work is closely related but builds on Bernanke's framework, and Bernanke is already a laureate. Restricting the award to the two originators gives a clean attribution.
assessment.maturity: The seminal paper is from 1997, with nearly three decades of extensions, empirical applications and policy use. It is clearly mature.
uncertainties: Direct empirical validation is mixed, since the mechanism is mostly established through calibrated models.
The relation to the 2022 banking and financial-crisis prize could be read as overlapping.
Whether Gertler or Gilchrist should be added is a judgement call.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework underpin the standard approach to monetary policy analysis, inflation targeting and central-bank practice. The impact on both theory and practice is very large.
assessment.attribution: Credit is widely distributed: Calvo (time-dependent pricing), Taylor (staggered contracts and the policy rule), Woodford (the integrated framework and optimal policy), plus Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets (estimation and empirical DSGE). The proposed trio covers the conceptual foundations, but any selection of three leaves out important contributors, which makes attribution the main difficulty.
assessment.maturity: The core ideas date from the 1980s through the early 2000s, with decades of use in policy institutions. It is clearly mature, and some recognition is arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Post-2008 and post-2021 critiques of DSGE models and of the inflation-forecasting record.
Strong attribution competition among the eight credited names.
Previous prizes (Lucas, Phelps, Sargent and Sims, Bernanke and others) touch adjacent ground.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The BLP demand-estimation approach and dynamic industry models made structural estimation of differentiated-product markets practical. It is now the workhorse for merger analysis, antitrust and regulatory evaluation, and the practical impact is large.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes produced the 1995 BLP framework, and Pakes also has major dynamic-game contributions (Ericson-Pakes). Bresnahan and others made adjacent contributions to empirical IO, so attribution is reasonably identifiable with a trio.
assessment.maturity: The seminal work is from the mid-1990s and has been used extensively for three decades, so it is mature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views the contribution as methodological or as a discovery about economic phenomena.
Competing credit for the broader empirical industrial organization program (Bresnahan, Reiss, Levin and others).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection reoriented international trade theory and empirics. They explain exporter productivity premia and the within-industry reallocation channel of the gains from trade, and they changed the quantitative evaluation of trade policy.
assessment.attribution: The Melitz (2003) model is the clear anchor. Helpman's contributions span trade with heterogeneous firms, the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple FDI results and earlier work. Redding is important mainly for quantitative extensions and geography. A pairing seems the most defensible, although other trade scholars could also be considered.
assessment.maturity: The core work is over twenty years old, with extensive follow-up and confirmation, so it is mature.
uncertainties: Krugman's 2008 prize partly covers the same intellectual ground (monopolistic competition and trade).
Helpman also appears in a separate political-economy trade candidate, which splits his credit.
Quantitative gains from firm heterogeneity are sensitive to modeling assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the empirical work on trade shocks reshaped understanding of wage inequality, polarization and the distributional effects of globalization and automation. The policy relevance is high.
assessment.attribution: The credited set mixes distinct contributions: skill-biased technical change and the education-technology race (Katz, with Goldin, a laureate), the task approach (Autor and co-authors), and the China shock (Autor, Dorn and Hanson). Acemoglu's task framework has already been recognized. Selecting three names requires choosing among overlapping lines.
assessment.maturity: The work spans the 1990s to the 2010s. The China shock literature is already well tested, though its interpretation continues to develop, so the field is mostly mature.
uncertainties: The magnitude and persistence of the China shock effects have been debated.
Overlap with the Goldin and Acemoglu prizes.
Attribution of the task framework across several authors, some outside the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Empirical work on adverse selection and moral hazard in insurance markets connected classical information-economics theory to real contract and claims data. It informs the design of health insurance and public policy, and it builds directly on the 2001 information economics prize.
assessment.attribution: Finkelstein and Einav developed much of the modern empirical framework for welfare and selection in insurance markets. Salanie contributed on the testing and theoretical side (with Chiappori). Others who worked on the early tests are not credited, so the credit story is plausible but not perfectly clean.
assessment.maturity: Most of the key papers are from 2000 to 2015, which is about one to two decades of confirmation. It is moderately mature, and it is less settled than the oldest candidates.
uncertainties: The foundations were already honored in 2001, so the marginal contribution is empirical and may be judged less novel.
Heterogeneous findings across markets about the importance of adverse selection.
Whether the field is considered mature enough for recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The law-and-finance literature showed empirically that legal systems and investor protection are tied to financial development and ownership structure. It opened a major research agenda in comparative corporate finance and institutions and influenced policy debate.
assessment.attribution: The legal-origins papers of La Porta, Lopez-de-Silanes, Shleifer and Vishny are collectively credited. Vishny has other distinct contributions, so the three-name selection reflects the legal-origins core but leaves one co-author out. Credit in this case is clear but somewhat arbitrary at the boundary.
assessment.maturity: The foundational papers are from 1997 to 2008 and have been replicated and challenged widely, so the timing is mature.
uncertainties: The legal-origins thesis has been strongly criticized on measurement and causal-identification grounds.
The relative weight of this versus other institutions research.
The omission of Vishny or a different three-person selection could be argued.
